newsitem.title: USA: No EU drive for single Euro bank regulator -- BoE.
newsitem.headline: No EU drive for single Euro bank regulator -- BoE.

text.p: European nations, despite their drive for a single currency and central bank, have no plans to set up a single European banking regulator, a senior Bank of England official said on Tuesday.

"There is as yet absolutely no pressure for supervision to be conducted within the European Union by an European economic area-wide supervisor," Michael Foot, executive director at the Bank of England, told a conference of the Bankers' Association for Foreign Trade.
"Quite the reverse, the European Central Bank... will have very little role to play in any supervisory matters," he added.

Foot said the banking industry in Europe will remain under the supervision of respective regulators in each European nation until "there is a unanimous request at the highest political level within the union" to create a single regulator.
Foot, who took part in a panel discussion about global regulation, declined to comment on the British government's decision on Tuesday to grant the Bank of England independence.

The Bank of England official said the globalization of financial services and the emergence of new products such as those generated on the Internet creates "more headaches for regulators" and raises the issue of "umbrella regulators."
While noting the benefits of international co-operation between regulators, Foot cautioned about several hurdles in the way of global banking regulation.

"Every country has at least some distinctive domestic code of conduct or other public good rules which are different from even its closest neighbors," Foot said, while noting Europe is the economic zone where the most efforts have been undertaken to reduce these differences.
"But even in the European economic area, there are still niggling host-country impediments to full-blown competition in too many countries," he acknowledged.

Commenting on the global impact of recent international failures in the banking sector, Foot noted this has led the Group of Ten and the International Monetary Fund to work on a "Code of Good Practive for banking supervisors the world over."

"What I do not see anywhere, and I do not expect to see for a long time, is any move to construct supervisory agencies on a global basis to monitor the global businesses that now confront us," Foot said.
The Bank of England director also pointed out that the United States is leading the move toward increased assessment of risk by banks themselves.
